1219.title: Chabad's open doors
1219.hook: Chabad centers worldwide welcome Jews of every background
1219.howItsDone: Chabad emissaries, often married couples, run Chabad houses and centers that host Shabbat meals, holiday events and classes open to Jews of any background, and offer passersby the chance to do a single commandment, like putting on tefillin.

segments.voice: Last week ended on tradition as home: Sephardi and Mizrahi synagogues open to a wide range of observance. Today, a Hasidic movement that made the open door its whole method.

A backpacker lands in a city on the far side of the world on a Friday afternoon. No plans, no friends, a phone at four percent. Someone at the hostel says: there's a Chabad house a few streets away, they do dinner. She goes, half expecting to be turned away for not knowing the prayers. Instead a young couple opens the door, pulls up another chair, and puts a bowl of soup in front of her. Nobody asks how observant she is. A child hands her a song sheet. Today is about that door.
screen: `FRIDAY, FAR FROM HOME.` → `A CHAIR PULLED UP.` → `NOBODY ASKS HOW OBSERVANT.`

segments.voice: Chabad's open doors. First, who they are. Chabad is a Hasidic movement, fully Orthodox, the line of Rabbi Shneur Zalman, whom you met among the Hasidic masters. The movement explains its name as three Hebrew words, chochmah, binah, da'at: wisdom, understanding, knowledge. Its teaching asks the mind to lead the heart. Second, the emissaries. Its leader, known simply as the Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, sent young couples out as shluchim, emissaries, to cities, campuses and far-off towns, to settle there and stay. A Chabad house is often their own home, with the dining table stretched long. Third, the welcome. A Chabad center doesn't ask a Jew to join, sign, or already keep the law before coming in. A Passover seder for anyone who shows up. Candles handed out on a Friday. A man on a busy sidewalk offered the chance to put on tefillin for a minute. The idea underneath: every single commandment, done once, by anyone, matters. Fourth, the oldest picture behind it. Genesis says Abraham "sat in the tent door in the heat of the day." When three strangers appeared, "he ran to meet them from the tent door." The rabbis told that Abraham's tent was open on all four sides, so a guest never had to look for the entrance. A Chabad house echoes that tent. Not every Jew shares Chabad's theology or style, and some argue with parts of it. Today is about the open door: a tent with its sides rolled up.

segments.voice: Picture a tent with all four sides rolled up. Then remember a time someone pulled up a chair for you, a meal you were invited to, a door that opened before you knocked: who was it, and what didn't they ask you? Stay a few breaths with what it was like to be let in, and if you pray, give thanks for that person.
Chabad's open doors. A Hasidic, Orthodox movement whose emissaries settle in towns and campuses and welcome Jews of every background, no test at the door. Today's word.
Your line: open doors. One extra chair can be a whole welcome. See you tomorrow.

1220.title: New roles in Orthodoxy
1220.hook: women scholars and leaders in Orthodox settings; the debates continue
1220.howItsDone: In some Orthodox communities, women study Talmud and halakha at advanced levels, serve as yoatzot halakha advising on family law, and hold teaching or leadership roles, while other Orthodox authorities oppose some of these roles.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: open doors, and Abraham running to meet three strangers. Today, a door inside Orthodoxy, and an argument about how far it opens.

The Talmud tells of a scholar named Rabbi Meir, troubled by some neighbors who made his life miserable. He prayed that they would die. His wife Beruriah stopped him. Read the psalm again, she said. It asks that sins be ended, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, and then there will be no more wicked people. Rabbi Meir prayed that way, the story says, and they turned. In the pages of the Talmud, a woman corrects a great sage's reading of a verse, and he listens.
screen: `RABBI MEIR'S PRAYER.` → `BERURIAH: SINS, NOT SINNERS.` → `HE LISTENS.`

segments.voice: New roles in Orthodoxy. Back on day one thousand forty-one, you met women rabbis and the Orthodox debate. Today, up close. First, the old voices. The Bible names women who taught and judged: "And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time." When the scroll of the law was found in the Temple, the king's men went to consult "Huldah the prophetess." And there's Beruriah, a teacher of Torah in the Talmud's own pages. Second, the new study halls. In recent generations, Orthodox women have taken up deep study of Talmud and halakha in their own study halls, and some now teach it at a high level. Third, new roles. One is the yoetzet halakha, a woman trained to advise on the laws of family and marriage that touch very private parts of life, so that women can ask a woman. Others serve congregations as scholars, teachers or spiritual leaders, under titles some communities have chosen carefully. Fourth, the debate, and it's a real one. Some Orthodox rabbis and bodies welcome these roles as faithful to halakha. Others hold that certain roles, especially the title rabbi, cross a line that tradition has kept, and say so firmly. Both sides argue from the same law and say they are protecting it. This lesson doesn't settle it. The argument is happening inside Orthodoxy, among people who hold halakha binding, which is why it matters so much to them. Beruriah's story is still taught in their study halls. What it means for today is exactly what they debate.

segments.voice: Bring back the yoetzet halakha, a woman someone can ask a private question of, quietly, and get an answer from the law. Then think of a role in your own world that someone stepped into for the first time, maybe your mother, a teacher, you: what did it cost them, and what did it open? Hold it gently, without deciding anything.
New roles in Orthodoxy. Women as scholars, advisers and leaders in Orthodox settings, from the yoetzet halakha to teachers of Talmud, and a debate about them that continues. Today's word.
Your line: new roles. Old voices, new rooms, an honest argument. I'll be here tomorrow.

1221.title: Conservative (Masorti) Judaism
1221.hook: halakha as binding, and developing through history
1221.howItsDone: Conservative and Masorti Jews hold halakha as binding while studying its historical development, and their rabbis rule on new questions from the traditional sources with that history in view.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: new roles. Women as scholars and advisers in Orthodox settings, and a debate inside the law about how far those roles reach. Today, a movement that answers the question of change differently.

Every seventh year, the Torah says, debts are released. A generous law. But the Mishnah tells what happened next: as the seventh year drew near, people stopped lending to the poor, afraid they would never be repaid. The Torah had warned against exactly that, the thought in the heart that says the year of release is at hand. So Hillel, the great sage, enacted the prozbul, a court document that kept loans collectible, so that lending would go on. The goal of the law was kept by changing how it worked. Today's movement points to that story.
screen: `DEBTS RELEASED IN THE SEVENTH YEAR.` → `PEOPLE STOP LENDING.` → `HILLEL'S PROZBUL.`

segments.voice: Masorti. It's the Hebrew word for traditional, from masoret, tradition. In North America the movement is called Conservative Judaism; in Israel and elsewhere, Masorti. First, halakha is binding. Conservative Judaism holds that Jewish law obligates Jews: Shabbat, kashrut, prayer, the festivals. That sets it apart from movements that see the law as guidance only. Second, the law has a history. Conservative scholars study how halakha grew: the Bible, the Mishnah, the Talmud, the codes, each generation adding and adjusting. They point to moments like Hillel's prozbul, where sages changed how a law worked in order to keep its purpose. Third, so the law can still develop. If it developed before, the movement holds, it may develop now, carefully, by rabbis trained in the sources, reasoning from inside the tradition, with history in view. Orthodox Judaism also answers new questions from inside the law, as you heard; the difference is in how far change may go, and who may make it. Fourth, the deep root. The tractate of the Fathers opens: Moses received the Torah and handed it on, masar, to Joshua. Masoret, tradition, is something handed on. Deuteronomy says: "ask thy father, and he will shew thee; thy elders, and they will tell thee." The movement hears in that a tradition both received and alive, passing through human hands, and shaped by them. Tomorrow, how those hands actually make decisions.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one habit or rule you started for a good reason: a budget, a morning routine, a house rule about phones at dinner. If it has, picture one small change that would serve the purpose better, the way Hillel's court document kept lending alive.
Masorti. Traditional: the name for Conservative Judaism in Israel and elsewhere, which holds halakha as binding and as developing through history. Today's word.

1222.title: The Law Committee
1222.hook: Conservative rabbis rule on questions like driving to synagogue on Shabbat
1222.howItsDone: In the Conservative movement, rabbis bring questions of Jewish law to the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, which answers in written responsa; each congregation's rabbi decides which approved answer the community follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Masorti, and your line: tradition and change, halakha as binding, and halakha with a history. Today, the room where rulings like that get made.

Saturday morning. A family is dressed for synagogue, but the building is across town, too far for the grandmother to walk, too far for the kids. The car sits in the driveway. For a family that keeps Shabbat, that car is a real question: Shabbat is a day without kindling fire, and rabbis have long treated starting an engine as part of that. Stay home and miss praying with their community? Or drive, only there and only back? In the Conservative movement, a question like that doesn't get settled at the kitchen table. It goes to a committee.
screen: `SATURDAY, A CAR IN THE DRIVEWAY.` → `TOO FAR TO WALK.` → `A QUESTION FOR THE COMMITTEE.`

segments.voice: The Law Committee. Its full name is the Committee on Jewish Law and Standards, and it belongs to the Conservative movement's association of rabbis. Its job is old work in a new room. Long before any committee, a Jew with a hard question of law wrote to a scholar, and the scholar wrote back. The answer is called a teshuvah, a response, and the committee writes teshuvot too: sources, arguments, a conclusion. The text behind the driving question is short. The Torah says, "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." The hard part was weighing two goods: Shabbat rest, and praying together. The committee's answer, as it is usually told, was that a family living too far to walk could drive to synagogue on Shabbat, and home again, and nowhere else. Not because Shabbat matters less, but because losing the community's prayer would cost Shabbat more. One more thing to know: the committee can approve more than one answer to the same question. Then each congregation's rabbi, called the mara d'atra, the master of the place, chooses which one that community follows. So some Conservative synagogues accepted the driving ruling, and some Conservative Jews still walk every Shabbat. Orthodox authorities hold that driving on Shabbat is forbidden, and they reach that answer from the same texts. Two movements, one Torah, different weighings.

segments.voice: Bring back the family and the car, and hold one good in each hand: a day of rest with no engine and no errands, and the grandmother and the kids praying together. Don't decide; just feel the weight of each, the way a committee has to. Then ask yourself which is harder: judging an answer, or writing one.

The Law Committee. The Conservative movement's committee that answers questions of Jewish law in writing, can approve more than one answer, and leaves the choice to each congregation's rabbi. Today's word.
Your line: law that develops. Two goods, weighed in writing, one answer at a time. See you tomorrow.

1223.title: Egalitarian
1223.hook: women counted in the minyan and ordained as rabbis
1223.howItsDone: In egalitarian synagogues, women and men are counted equally in the minyan, are called to the Torah and lead services, and women serve as rabbis and cantors; other congregations keep the traditional practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Law Committee, and the family with the car in the driveway. Your line: law that develops. Today, another question that same committee took up.

A weekday morning, early, in a small chapel. Prayer books are out, a few people are wrapped in prayer shawls, someone keeps checking the door. Some prayers can only be said with a full quorum, a minyan, and they are waiting to begin. A woman sits in the second row. She knows every word of the service; she came to say the mourner's prayer for her father. In some synagogues, she is the one who makes the quorum complete. In others, the room is still waiting. Same prayers, same morning, a different count.
screen: `AN EARLY MORNING CHAPEL.` → `WAITING FOR A MINYAN.` → `DOES SHE COUNT?`

segments.voice: Egalitarian. It means equal, and in Jewish life it names a community where women and men take the same roles in prayer and leadership. You met the minyan on day seventeen: a count of ten, so some prayers are never said alone. The Mishnah lists prayers not said with fewer than ten, and in traditional halakha those ten are men. Women pray too, at home and in synagogue, but they were not counted, did not lead the public service, and were not ordained as rabbis. Then the change. The Conservative movement's Law Committee took up the question in writing and approved counting women in the minyan. Later the movement's seminary began ordaining women as rabbis and cantors. The Reform and Reconstructionist movements ordain women too. But remember yesterday's rule: the committee can approve more than one answer, and the local rabbi chooses. So Conservative and Masorti congregations went different ways: some became egalitarian, and some stayed with the traditional practice. Orthodox communities keep the traditional minyan of men, and some have opened new roles for women within it, as you heard three days ago. Some who argued for the change pointed to the Torah's first chapter: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Those who held to the tradition answered from the long body of law on the minyan. Both sides argued from texts. And for the woman in the second row, it's concrete: in an egalitarian room, when she walks in, someone at the door says, ten.

1224.title: Masorti worldwide
1224.hook: Masorti communities in Israel, Europe and Latin America
1224.howItsDone: Masorti communities in Israel, Europe and Latin America pray in Hebrew, teach and preach in local languages, and follow the Conservative approach to halakha, with rabbis trained in seminaries such as those in Jerusalem and Buenos Aires.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was egalitarian: the woman in the second row, and the voice at the door saying ten. Today, the same movement, far from where it began.

Friday evening in Buenos Aires. The street is loud, the synagogue is louder. Families crowd in, kids slide along the benches, someone is already humming the tune before the cantor starts. The prayers are in Hebrew, the same words said in Jerusalem and London tonight. But the rabbi's welcome is in Spanish, and so are the jokes during the announcements. Afterward, out on the sidewalk, people say Shabbat shalom and then switch to arguing about football. Nobody here calls their synagogue Conservative. They use another word, the one you met three days ago.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT, BUENOS AIRES.` → `HEBREW PRAYERS, SPANISH WELCOME.` → `NOT CONSERVATIVE. MASORTI.`

segments.voice: Masorti worldwide. Masorti is Hebrew for traditional, and outside North America it is the name this movement goes by. The approach is the one you've been learning: halakha as binding, and halakha that develops, with rabbis reasoning from the sources and congregations choosing among approved answers. Now take it on a short trip. First, Latin America. In Buenos Aires a rabbinical seminary trains rabbis to teach and lead in Spanish and Portuguese, so a community in South America can be led by someone who grew up in its own language. Second, Israel. There the official rabbinate is Orthodox, and Masorti congregations build their life alongside it: their own synagogues, schools and rabbis, often trained in Jerusalem. Keeping tradition in Hebrew, at home, while asking for a place in the public square. Third, Europe. In Britain and on the continent there are Masorti synagogues, some large, some small enough that everyone knows who brought the cake. Each one sounds like where it is: the accents differ, the tunes differ, the food after services differs. What travels is the method: take the law seriously, and let it develop. A psalm says it in one line: "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth." All the earth, in many accents.

1225.title: Reform Judaism
1225.hook: ethics and informed personal choice at the center; tradition as a guide
1225.howItsDone: Reform Jews treat the Torah's ethical commandments as central and approach ritual as a guide: individuals and congregations study practices like Shabbat, kashrut and prayer, then choose which to observe.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: worldwide, Masorti in Buenos Aires, Jerusalem and Europe. This week ran from Chabad's open doors and new roles in Orthodoxy, through Masorti, the Law Committee and egalitarian prayer. Today it ends with another movement.

segments.voice: What would you keep, if nobody required it of you? A man sits at a kitchen table with three books open and a mug going cold. He grew up lighting candles on Friday night because his mother did. Now he has his own kitchen, and nobody is going to check. So he is reading: what the Torah says about Shabbat, what the rabbis said, what his own congregation teaches. By the end of the evening he hasn't decided everything. But the candles stay, and he knows why. Today, the movement that puts that kitchen table at the center.
screen: `WHAT WOULD YOU KEEP?` → `THREE BOOKS AND A COLD MUG.` → `THE CANDLES STAY.`

segments.voice: Reform Judaism. Bring back the three questions from earlier in this block: revelation, how binding halakha is, and how change happens. Here are Reform's answers, the way the movement describes itself. First, ethics at the center. For Reform Jews, the heart of the Torah is its moral teaching: justice, honesty, care for the stranger and the poor. Those commandments are not optional. Second, revelation keeps going. God's will is not only something given once, but something each generation keeps understanding, so the tradition can grow. Third, today's line: informed choice. Rituals like Shabbat, the dietary laws and daily prayer are treated as a guide, not as binding law. Each Jew is asked to study them, then decide what to take on. The word informed matters. It isn't do whatever you like. It's learn first, then choose, exactly what the man at the kitchen table is doing. Some Reform teachers point to a line from Deuteronomy, where Moses sets the choice before the people: "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life." A choice, made with eyes open. Other movements weigh this differently. Orthodox Jews hold halakha as binding; Conservative Jews hold it as binding and developing. Reform places the decision in the hands of the person who has studied. Three answers, three serious ways to hold one tradition.
screen: `ETHICS AT THE CENTER.` · `REVELATION KEEPS GOING.` · `RITUAL AS A GUIDE.` · `LEARN FIRST, THEN CHOOSE.` · then, large: `THEREFORE CHOOSE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one habit you keep without thinking: a word you say, a meal you skip, a ritual from your family or your own life. Ask three questions, slowly: where did this come from, what is it for, do I still want it? You don't need to change anything; just know why you keep it, or why you'd let it go.
Reform Judaism. The movement that puts ethics at the center, sees revelation as ongoing, and treats ritual as a guide each Jew studies and then chooses from. Today's word.
